catalog_quote: There is an interesting distribution of consonants and vowels among the various languages of the Bole-Tangale group, which somehow goes along with their geographical location as there is a steady increase of consonants and vowels from the northern towards the southern located languages. This also holds for the tones. Nearly all languages exposed to the neighbourhood of Benue-Congo languages in the South show a kind of a ‘tone levelling‘ or ‘tone equalizing’ towards a ‘[frozen] low tone’ in most of the cases – be it in the lexicon or in the overwhelming part of the grammar – just contrary to the languages spoken in ‘Chadic’ environment, i.e. in the North and the East, where the flexibility of tone plays an important role in the grammar. sweep_summary: Kholok (khol1240, Widala/Kode, West Chadic, Bole-Tangale) is not in the catalog. The two stress-title items are one and the same paper, Xu, Chen & Wang 2012 (The Linguistic Review 29: 131-147, DOI 10.1515/tlr-2012-0006), held twice in Glottolog. An open author copy was downloaded from Yi Xu's UCL homepage and read in full: it studies post-focus compression in Taiwanese, Taiwan Mandarin and Beijing Mandarin and never mentions Kholok, Widala, Chadic or Nigeria; Glottolog attached it to khol1240 through the title word 'compression' (the language's Glottolog reference set carries 15 unrelated 'compression' titles beside Jungraithmayr & Leger 1993 'zone of ethnic and linguistic compression'). Relevance: other language; priority none. Beyond the works with stress in the title, the open Kholok-bearing sources held by the project (Baldi & Leger 2020 p. 47; Baldi & Leger 2011 pp. 30, 32; Jungraithmayr & Leger 1993 pp. 166-168) say only that Widala/Kholok is a tone language with tone levelling toward a frozen low tone and give tone-marked forms; none states word stress, so no new stress statement was found. The likely best phonology/tonology description, Leger 2014 (Fading Delimitations, pp. 229-261, tonology pp. 230-234), is paywalled at Koppe (priority high); Leger 2004 (De Gruyter, paywalled) and Leger 2000 (Festschrift Brann, print only) are medium.info domain now serves an unrelated site.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kholok (Widala) is treated as a lexical tone language (all forms transcribed with H/L tone, e.g. vùlùm 'knee', càkhì/càkhù 3sg pronouns, pèemò); the only prosodic generalisation offered is that the southern Bole-Tangale languages, Widala among them, show levelling of tone toward low tone. No statement about word stress or accent placement is made anywhere in the accessible literature.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the tone-levelling remark is a group-level tendency, not a Kholok-specific rule
new_statements.domain_note: Group-level comparative remark by the fieldworker (Leger) covering 'southern' Bole-Tangale languages listed as Tangale, Pero, Piya, Widala, Kushi, Nyam; detailed treatment deferred to Leger 2014: 230-234 (not accessible).
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand data on this language in print come from Rudolf Leger's fieldwork and are published under the name 'Widala' (also 'Widala-Kholok', 'Kode'); Widala/Kode is the people's autonym, Kholok [ktc, khol1240] is the Chadic language of one Widala section (the other section speaks Maghdi [gmd], Adamawa). The quoted passages refer to 'Widala' = Kholok.
